title: The Wardrobe of the old quarter
premise: Rosalind Whitlock, a piano tuner who reads a house's history through its radiators and pipes, inherits her late aunt's flat in the old quarter — along with an unfinished song she recognizes the moment it plays on the radio: a melody written by her aunt's lover decades ago and never recorded. As the estate sale deadline looms, Rosalind discovers the song was stolen, its author erased from the building's story by the very family now buying the property. Tuning the building room by room, she gathers testimony from tenants, ledgers, and the radiators themselves, and must choose between a clean sale that buries the truth and a public reckoning that costs her everything. In the end she refuses to sign, restores the composer's name to the deed of memory, and plays the finished song in the emptied parlor as the new owners walk away.
about_author: E. M. Ravensworth is the pen name of a former piano restorer who spent fifteen years tuning instruments in tenement buildings across northern port cities before turning to fiction. They write about objects that remember what people would rather forget.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Rosalind arrives at Aunt Vera's flat to catalog the estate, tuning the old upright and listening to the radiators' complaints like a language. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: grief disguised as professionalism; the first hint that this house speaks.

chapters.title: A Song on the Frequency
chapters.summary: In a café, a late-night radio program airs an untitled piece Rosalind knows was never recorded — Vera's composition, played from a handwritten score. She traces the broadcast to a community station. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past announcing itself in public.

chapters.title: The Buyer with Clean Hands
chapters.summary: Julian Marsh, representing the Halloway development group, visits with a generous offer and a ninety-day closing date. He is courteous, impatient, and oddly knowledgeable about the building's layout. POV: Julian. Emotional beat: charm with something underneath it.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Tuning radiators on the third floor, Rosalind finds initials scratched inside a panel: T.A., 1971. A tenant, Mrs. Okonkwo, mentions a composer who once lived there and 'left without his coat.' POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: Theodore Ansel's Coat
chapters.summary: Rosalind searches city archives for Theodore Ansel and finds a single credit on an obscure 1972 recording — then nothing. The score in Vera's drawer bears both their names, one crossed out. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: the crossed-out name as a wound she can't stop touching.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Julian pressures for early signature, offering to waive inspection contingencies. Rosalind stalls, citing the piano. He notices the sheet music on the stand and goes very still. POV: Julian. Emotional beat: fear leaking through composure.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Over bitter tea, Mrs. Okonkwo recounts 1971: Theodore and Vera rehearsing through the walls, then Theodore evicted after a fire no one could prove he set. POV: alternating recollection within Rosalind's frame. Emotional beat: belonging — a tenant testifying for a tenant.

chapters.title: The Fire Report
chapters.summary: Rosalind obtains the 1971 fire report: origin listed as 'electrical, probable,' signed off by an inspector named Halloway. The same family name as her buyer. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: cold clarity; justice outside the law begins here.

chapters.title: Ansel, Alive, Somewhere
chapters.summary: A retired session musician remembers Theodore moving north, playing hotel lounges under another name. Rosalind mails a letter to the last address on file, knowing it may go nowhere. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: hope handled carefully, like glass.

chapters.title: The Offer She Can't Refuse
chapters.summary: Julian raises the price substantially and hints that contested estates attract delays, liens, and lawyers. He asks directly whether Vera left papers. POV: Julian. Emotional beat: menace wearing a suit; Rosalind feels the trap close.

chapters.title: Vera's Letters
chapters.summary: Behind the radiator panel with the initials, Rosalind finds letters between Vera and Theodore — love, then his eviction, then his silence. The last letter is unopened, returned undelivered. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: inheritance redefined; she has been holding the wrong things.

chapters.title: The Unopened Letter
chapters.summary: Rosalind reads Vera's final letter: an apology, an admission that she stayed silent about the fire to keep the flat, and the unfinished song enclosed. POV: Vera, in letter-voice framed by Rosalind. Emotional beat: shame across generations; the cost of belonging bought unjustly.

chapters.title: A Reply from the North
chapters.summary: A phone call: an old man's voice asking who is asking about Theodore Ansel. He will not say yes or no, only that he'll be passing through the city in three weeks. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: trembling anticipation; the clock and the calendar aligning against the sale.

chapters.title: Delay Tactics
chapters.summary: Rosalind hires a surveyor to contest the property line, buying weeks. Julian retaliates by pulling the building's heat permit, threatening tenant displacement. POV: Julian. Emotional beat: escalation; the fight stops being about paper.

chapters.title: The Tenants Organize
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okonkwo convenes the remaining residents; they compile their own history of the building — rents paid, repairs withheld, names erased. Rosalind offers her inventory skills. POV: ensemble through Rosalind. Emotional beat: solidarity; the house's people become its chorus.

chapters.title: The Man at the Door
chapters.summary: Three weeks later, an elderly man stands in the parlor, hat in hand. Theodore Ansel listens to Rosalind play the unfinished song and corrects the third bar from memory. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: recognition; forty years collapse into four minutes of music.

chapters.title: What He Witnessed
chapters.summary: Theodore tells the whole story: the fire set to clear him out, the inspector bought, Vera's silence, his choice not to fight because fighting meant losing everything faster. He never stopped writing. POV: Theodore. Emotional beat: dignity without bitterness; grief finally spoken aloud.

chapters.title: Closing Date
chapters.summary: Julian learns Theodore is alive and in the building. He offers Rosalind double, then threatens litigation over the 'stolen' score. Rosalind realizes the Halloways' claim depends on Theodore staying legally invisible. POV: Julian. Emotional beat: desperation; the buyer's clean hands are filthy.

chapters.title: The Hearing Nobody Planned
chapters.summary: At the closing, instead of signing, Rosalind presents the letters, the fire report, and Theodore himself. The title company halts the sale pending investigation; the tenants' documented grievances surface simultaneously. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: climax; quiet people refusing quietly, and being heard.

chapters.title: What the Law Won't Do
chapters.summary: No court will restore what was taken in 1971, but the sale collapses, the Halloway group withdraws, and a local journalist runs the story. Theodore declines damages; he wants only the credit. POV: Theodore. Emotional beat: justice measured in acknowledgment, not money.

chapters.title: Recording Session, Parlor Floor
chapters.summary: The community station records Theodore and Rosalind performing the completed song in the emptied flat, radiators ticking like a metronome. The broadcast credits both composers. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: restoration; the unsaid finally said, on air.

chapters.title: The New Inventory
chapters.summary: Rosalind keeps the flat, takes tenants as clients, and begins a fresh ledger — this one listing everything said aloud. On the last page she writes Theodore's name where Vera's crossed-out version used to be. POV: Rosalind. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, inherited honestly at last.
